**Economic Inequality Widening**
Inequality has risen sharply across U.S. [Source: ev-1]
cities since the 1980s, reaching record levels by 2018–2021 according to Federal Reserve data tracking over 3,140 inequality series [Source: ev-1].
The national Gini coefficient reached 0.40 in 2013, but major metropolitan areas exhibit significantly higher disparity [Source: ev-1].

Specific city-level metrics include:
*   **New York City:** Gini coefficient of 0.5469 [Source: ev-1]
*   **Atlanta and Miami:** Gini coefficients of approximately 0.57 [Source: ev-1]
*   **New Orleans:** Gini coefficient of 0.56 [Source: ev-1]

Income ratios further illustrate this divide.
Several metros show income ratios reaching 18:1 between the top (95th percentile) and bottom (20th percentile) earners, including Atlanta and Washington D.C.[Source: ev-1].

The 80/20 income ratio is highest in New Orleans at 7.87, meaning the 80th percentile earns nearly eight times more than the 20th percentile; Boston follows closely at 7.81, with specific incomes of $172,476 for the 80th percentile versus $22,095 for the 20th [Source: ev-1].

claims.text: Historically, 57 of the 100 largest metropolitan areas saw significantly higher inequality in 2014 compared to 2007 [Source: ev-1].
In San Francisco, top incomes rose by approximately $120,000 between 2014 and 2016, while bottom quintile gains remained minimal across all cities [Source: ev-1].

**Affordability Crisis**
Urban nominal income growth has not kept pace with housing costs. [Source: ev-1]
Since 2000, home prices increased by 177%, while median household income grew only 92% [Source: ev-1].
The Case-Shiller Index reached 325.78 in July 2024, representing a 225% increase since January 2000 [Source: ev-1].
This divergence is most acute on the West Coast; California cities exhibit price-to-income ratios between 9.6 and 12.2, more than double the national average of 4.7 [Source: ev-1].

claims.text: Educational gentrification is also evident, with urban areas now having 35% of residents holding bachelor's degrees or higher, compared to 31% in suburbs and 19% in rural areas [Source: ev-1].

**Labor Market Transformation**
The economic base of cities shifted from manufacturing to services. [Source: ev-1]
Manufacturing jobs fell from 19.5 million in 1979 to under 11.5 million during the pandemic, while finance and professional services grew from 12 million to 32 million jobs [Source: ev-1].

This shift concentrated high-income professionals in urban cores, contributing to income polarization where urban centers house both top earners and low-wage service workers, unlike the more moderate distributions found in suburbs [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-2].

**Economic Mobility Decline**
Despite nominal wealth growth, economic mobility for lower-income families has worsened. [Source: ev-1]
Data indicates that 48 of the 50 largest metros experienced worsening economic mobility over a 15-year period (comparing cohorts growing up in the 1990s versus those from the 1980) [Source: ev-1].
Only Houston showed improvement, with a mere 1.1% gain in income outcomes [Source: ev-1].
